lessons.title: Sources of Trade Finance
lessons.body:
When you export from Africa, you often need money upfront to produce or buy goods, but buyers want to pay later. That gap is what trade finance fills. The most common source is your bank. In Nigeria, for example, Access Bank offers pre-export finance where they advance up to 70% of your confirmed order value. You repay from the export proceeds. Banks also issue letters of credit (LCs) which guarantee payment if you ship on time. But LCs cost 1-2% of the order value, and many small African exporters find them expensive.

Development finance institutions (DFIs) are another key source. The African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) runs a trade finance programme specifically for small businesses. They provide guarantees and direct loans from $50,000 upwards. The Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit (ICIEC) offers Sharia-compliant financing. In East Africa, the East African Development Bank (EADB) funds cross-border trade in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Rwanda.

Supplier credit is simpler: your supplier gives you 30-90 days to pay after you receive the goods. This works if you have a strong relationship. Buyer credit is the opposite: your buyer pays a deposit (often 30%) and the rest on delivery. For exports to Europe, you might use factoring companies like Ghanaâs Fenix International, which buy your invoices at a discount.

Microfinance banks and fintechs are emerging. In Kenya, Tugende and Asante Finance provide working capital for export orders under $10,000. They charge 2-4% per month, but approval takes days, not weeks. Finally, consider export credit agencies (ECAs) like South Africaâs ECIC or Indiaâs EXIM Bank. They insure and finance exports, but usually require you to be a registered company with at least two years of financial statements.

Start by asking your bank for a pre-shipment finance facility. If rejected, try Afreximbankâs trade finance window or a DFI. Always compare total cost: interest + fees + insurance. A 12% annual rate sounds high, but if you only need the money for 90 days, the actual cost is 3%.

lessons.title: Export Factoring and Forfaiting
lessons.body:
Export factoring and forfaiting are two ways to get cash immediately after you ship, without waiting 30, 60, or 90 days for your buyer to pay. They both involve selling your receivables to a third party at a discount, but they work differently.

Factoring is for short-term invoices, usually up to 90 days. You sell your invoice to a factor, who pays you 80-90% of the value upfront. When your buyer pays, the factor sends you the remaining 10-20%, minus a fee. For example, if you export $50,000 of cocoa to a Dutch buyer on 60-day terms, a factor might advance you $42,500 today, then $6,500 when the buyer pays, keeping $1,000 as a 2% fee. In Africa, factors include the African Export-Import Bankâs factoring programme and private firms like Factoring Africa in Kenya. Factoring is ideal for small exporters with many small invoices. It requires no collateral, but you need clean invoices and a reliable buyer.

Forfaiting is for larger, longer-term receivables, often 180 days to 5 years. You sell a promissory note or bill of exchange (guaranteed by a bank) to a forfaiter at a discount. There is no recourse to you if the buyer defaults. For instance, you export $500,000 of machinery to a Nigerian buyer with a 2-year payment plan. A forfaiter might buy the notes for $450,000, giving you cash now. Forfaiting is common in capital goods and project exports. In Africa, forfaiting is offered by banks like Standard Bank and Rand Merchant Bank. The cost is higher than factoring: 8-15% discount rate depending on country risk.

Key differences: Factoring is short-term, often with recourse (you may have to buy back the invoice if the buyer doesnât pay). Forfaiting is long-term, without recourse. Factoring fees are 1-3% per month; forfaiting discounts are 8-15% per year. Both require you to have a buyer with good credit. If you are a small African exporter, start with factoring. Itâs easier to access and cheaper for small amounts. For large contracts, ask your bank about forfaiting.

lessons.title: Currency Hedging Techniques
lessons.body:
If you export from Africa, you often get paid in US dollars or euros, but your costs are in local currency. If the exchange rate moves against you, your profit can vanish. For example, you agree to sell $10,000 of coffee at 100 KES per dollar, expecting 1,000,000 KES. But by the time you get paid, the rate is 110 KES per dollar, so you only get 1,100,000 KES? Wait, thatâs more. Actually, if the dollar weakens, you get less. Suppose the rate moves to 90 KES per dollar: you get 900,000 KES, losing 100,000 KES. Hedging protects you from this.

The simplest hedge is a forward contract. You lock in an exchange rate today for a future date. Your bank agrees to sell you dollars at, say, 100 KES in 90 days. When you receive your export payment, you exchange at that rate, no matter what the market does. Most African banks offer forwards for amounts above $10,000, with a small deposit. For smaller amounts, use a money transfer operator like Mukuru or WorldRemit that offers fixed rates for 24 hours.

Another tool is a currency option. You pay a premium (1-3% of the amount) for the right, but not the obligation, to exchange at a set rate. If the rate moves in your favour, you let the option expire and use the market rate. Options are useful if youâre unsure about the exact payment date. Banks like Ecobank and Absa offer options in Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa.

For very small businesses, consider invoicing in your local currency. Many African buyers will accept this. Or use a multi-currency account like those from Flutterwave or Payoneer, which let you hold dollars and convert when the rate is good. You can also ask for a deposit in dollars and the balance in local currency to split risk.

Finally, natural hedging: if you also import supplies, your dollar income can pay for your dollar imports, reducing exposure. Always calculate your break-even exchange rate and set a forward contract if the current rate is close to it. Donât gamble on currency; hedge what you can.

lessons.title: Political and Country Risk Assessment
lessons.body:
When you export to another country, you face risks beyond your buyerâs credit: the government might change rules, block payments, or seize goods. This is political and country risk. For African exporters, this is real. In 2020, Nigeria closed its borders, and many Ghanaian exporters lost goods. In 2022, the coup in Burkina Faso disrupted trade routes. You need to assess these risks before you ship.

Start with a country risk rating. Agencies like Moodyâs, S&P, and Fitch rate countries from AAA (safe) to D (default). You can find free summaries on Trading Economics or the World Bankâs Doing Business reports. For example, as of 2024, Botswana is rated A- (low risk), while Zimbabwe is D (high risk). The African Development Bank also publishes a country risk index.

Next, look at specific political factors: upcoming elections, civil unrest, currency controls, and corruption. The World Bankâs Worldwide Governance Indicators give scores for political stability, rule of law, and control of corruption. If a country scores below 30th percentile, be cautious. Also check if the country is on the FATF grey list for money laundering, which can delay payments.

Use export credit agencies (ECAs) to cover political risk. South Africaâs ECIC, Indiaâs EXIM Bank, and Chinaâs Sinosure offer political risk insurance. For example, ECIC will insure up to 90% of your export value against war, expropriation, and transfer restrictions. The premium is 0.5-2% of the contract value. The Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit (ICIEC) covers similar risks for OIC countries.

If you canât get insurance, use payment terms that reduce risk: require a letter of credit confirmed by a bank in a stable country (like a UK or French bank). Or ask for payment in advance for first orders. For large projects, consider a joint venture with a local partner to navigate political networks.

Always have a contingency plan: if a countryâs risk spikes, pause shipments and find alternative buyers. Monitor news from Reuters, Bloomberg, and local sources. Political risk is manageable if you do your homework.

lessons.title: Credit Risk Management
lessons.body:
Credit risk is the chance your buyer wonât pay. In international trade, you often donât know your buyer well, and chasing debts across borders is expensive. So you must manage credit risk before you ship. Start by asking for trade references from your buyerâs other suppliers. Call them and ask: did they pay on time? Were there disputes? Also request a bank reference letter. In Africa, banks like Standard Chartered and Ecobank can provide this.

Next, run a credit report. Companies like Dun & Bradstreet, Creditsafe, and Coface sell reports for $50-$200. For African buyers, you can also use local credit bureaus: TransUnion in South Africa, Creditinfo in Kenya, and CRC in Nigeria. The report shows payment history, legal disputes, and financial health. If the report shows a poor score, demand a letter of credit (LC) or advance payment.

Set credit limits for each buyer. A common rule: donât extend credit beyond 10% of your monthly export sales to any one buyer. For new buyers, start with a small trial order (e.g., $5,000) and require 50% deposit. If they pay on time, increase the limit gradually. Use credit insurance for larger orders. Providers like ATI (African Trade Insurance Agency) and Euler Hermes cover up to 90% of losses if a buyer defaults. The premium is 0.3-1% of the insured amount.

If you sell on open account (no LC), offer a discount for early payment: 2% off if paid within 10 days. This improves cash flow and reduces risk. Also, use a promissory note or bill of exchange signed by the buyer, which is legally enforceable in many countries. If a buyer is late, act fast: send a reminder after 5 days, call after 15 days, and involve a collection agency after 30 days. In Africa, collection agencies like African Trade Collections work across borders.

Finally, diversify. Donât rely on one buyer or one country. If a buyer defaults, you still have others. And always keep a reserve fund of 5% of annual export sales to cover bad debts.

lessons.title: Using Trade Insurance
lessons.body:
Trade insurance protects you from non-payment by your buyer, whether due to bankruptcy, refusal to pay, or political events. Itâs like health insurance for your export business. In Africa, several providers offer trade insurance tailored to small exporters. The African Trade Insurance Agency (ATI) is the largest, covering 20+ countries. ATI insures up to 90% of your invoice value, with premiums starting at 0.3% for low-risk buyers. For example, if you export $100,000 to a buyer in Rwanda, you might pay $300-$500 for coverage. If the buyer defaults, ATI pays you $90,000 and then chases the buyer themselves.

Other providers include the Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit (ICIEC), which covers OIC countries, and South Africaâs ECIC for exports from South Africa. Private insurers like Coface, Euler Hermes, and Atradius also cover African risks, but they often require larger volumes (above $500,000 per year).

How to get covered? First, apply to an insurer with your buyerâs details and your export contract. The insurer will assess the buyerâs credit and the country risk. If approved, you pay a premium (either a one-time fee or a monthly charge). You must report all shipments under the policy and pay premiums on each. If a buyer doesnât pay within 90-180 days, you file a claim. The insurer then pays you and takes over collection.

Trade insurance also helps you get financing. Banks are more willing to lend against insured receivables. For example, in Kenya, banks like KCB accept ATI-insured invoices as collateral for up to 80% of the value. This solves your cash flow problem.

But note: insurance doesnât cover disputes over quality or late delivery. You must still ship on time and meet contract terms. Also, you usually have to bear a deductible (10% of the loss). Always read the policy exclusions. For small exporters, ATIâs âSmall and Medium Enterprisesâ programme is a good start. It costs as little as $200 per year for coverage up to $50,000. Contact ATI or your bankâs trade finance department to apply.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common source of pre-export finance for small African exporters?
quiz.explanation: Afreximbank provides trade finance specifically for African businesses, including small exporters.

quiz.q: What is the typical advance rate for export factoring?
quiz.explanation: Factors usually advance 80-90% of the invoice value upfront, with the balance after buyer payment.

quiz.q: Forfaiting is best suited for:
quiz.explanation: Forfaiting handles larger, longer-term receivables (180 days to 5 years) without recourse.

quiz.q: Which hedging tool locks in an exchange rate for a future date?
quiz.explanation: A forward contract fixes the exchange rate today for a future transaction.

quiz.q: What does a currency option give you?
options: A) Obligation to exchange at a set rate
B) Right but not obligation to exchange at a set rate
quiz.explanation: An option gives the right, not the obligation, to exchange at a specified rate, for a premium.

quiz.q: Which agency provides political risk insurance for African exports?
quiz.explanation: ATI offers political risk and credit insurance for African trade.

quiz.q: What is a common indicator of country risk?
quiz.explanation: Credit ratings from agencies like Moody's assess a country's ability and willingness to pay debts.

quiz.q: Which of these is a way to manage credit risk?
options: B) Setting credit limits per buyer
quiz.explanation: Setting credit limits helps control exposure to any single buyer.

quiz.q: What does trade insurance typically cover?
quiz.explanation: Trade insurance covers non-payment due to buyer default or political events, not quality disputes.

quiz.q: Which African bank offers pre-export finance?
quiz.explanation: Access Bank in Nigeria provides pre-export finance to exporters.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between factoring and forfaiting?
options: A) Factoring is long-term, forfaiting is short-term
B) Factoring is short-term, forfaiting is long-term
D) Forfaiting is only for local sales
quiz.explanation: Factoring handles short-term invoices (up to 90 days), while forfaiting handles longer-term receivables.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural hedge?
options: B) Having both exports and imports in same currency
quiz.explanation: Natural hedging matches foreign currency income with foreign currency expenses.

quiz.q: What is the FATF grey list?
options: B) List of countries with weak anti-money laundering controls
C) List of countries with high tariffs
D) List of countries with free trade
quiz.explanation: The FATF grey list identifies countries with strategic deficiencies in combating money laundering.

quiz.q: Which of these is a credit reference source?
quiz.explanation: Dun & Bradstreet provides credit reports on businesses.

quiz.q: What is a promissory note?
options: A) A legal document where buyer promises to pay
quiz.explanation: A promissory note is a written promise to pay a specified sum on a certain date.

quiz.q: Which agency insures exports from South Africa?
quiz.explanation: The Export Credit Insurance Corporation (ECIC) of South Africa provides export credit insurance.

quiz.q: What is a common premium range for trade insurance?
quiz.explanation: Trade insurance premiums typically range from 0.3% to 1% of the insured value.

quiz.q: Which of these is a political risk?
quiz.explanation: Currency transfer restrictions are a political risk imposed by governments.

quiz.q: What should you do if a buyer is late paying?
options: B) Send reminder after 5 days, call after 15, involve collection after 30
quiz.explanation: A structured escalation process helps recover debts efficiently.

quiz.q: Which of these is a multi-currency account provider?
quiz.explanation: Flutterwave offers multi-currency accounts for African businesses.

quiz.q: What is the role of export credit agencies (ECAs)?
options: A) Provide insurance and financing for exports
quiz.explanation: ECAs support exports by providing insurance, guarantees, and financing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a forfaiting provider in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Standard Bank offers forfaiting services in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of trade insurance for financing?
options: A) Banks accept insured receivables as collateral
D) It removes need for contracts
quiz.explanation: Insured receivables are more acceptable to banks as collateral for loans.

quiz.q: Which of these is a source of trade finance for small exporters?
quiz.explanation: Microfinance banks provide working capital for small export orders.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a letter of credit?
quiz.explanation: Letters of credit usually cost 1-2% of the order value in fees.

quiz.q: Which of these is a political risk assessment tool?
quiz.explanation: World Bank Governance Indicators score countries on political stability, rule of law, etc.

quiz.q: What is a common credit limit rule for new buyers?
options: B) Start with small trial order and require deposit
quiz.explanation: Starting small with a deposit reduces risk for new buyers.

quiz.q: Which of these is a trade insurance provider?
quiz.explanation: Coface is a global trade credit insurer.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a forward contract?
quiz.explanation: A forward contract locks in an exchange rate for a future date to hedge currency risk.

quiz.q: Which of these is a way to reduce political risk?
options: A) Require confirmed letter of credit from stable country bank
quiz.explanation: A confirmed LC from a stable bank reduces political and credit risk.
